cards.t: Anemia and the red cell indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW)
q: what is anemia
what does mean corpuscular volume tell you
what is red cell distribution width
what are the normal red cell indices
cards.x:
Anemia is a drop in the amount of healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin, which lowers the blood's ability to carry oxygen to the tissues. The red cell indices on a complete blood count describe what the cells look like:

- Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): the average size of the red cells, 80 to 100 femtoliters (fL).
- Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH): how much hemoglobin sits in each cell, 27 to 31 picograms per cell.
- Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC): hemoglobin relative to the size of each cell, 32 to 36 g/dL.
- Red cell distribution width (RDW): how much the cells differ in size. Healthy red cells are usually about the same size, so a high RDW means a mix of sizes.

Hemoglobin is the amount of hemoglobin in the blood; hematocrit is the percentage of the blood volume taken up by red cells.

cards.t: Initial approach to anemia: history, complete blood count and reticulocyte index
q: how do you start working up an anemia
what do you look at on the complete blood count in anemia
why check the reticulocyte index
what does size of the red cells tell you
cards.x:
Start with the history and physical, which may already point toward a diagnosis. Then read the complete blood count (CBC) in three steps.

First, look at all three cell lines: red cells, white cells and platelets, and ask whether all of them are low, which is called pancytopenia. Second, look at the mean corpuscular volume (MCV), the average red cell size. Small cells point you to the microcytic anemias, and large cells point you to the macrocytic anemias. Third, check the reticulocyte index to judge whether the bone marrow is responding adequately to the anemia.

So size sorts the anemias into two big families, and the reticulocyte index tells you whether the marrow is keeping up.

cards.t: Causes of iron deficiency anemia
k: why do people get iron deficiency
q: what causes iron deficiency anemia
what is the most common cause of iron deficiency in adults
which medications cause iron deficiency
cards.x:
Iron deficiency has four groups of causes.

- Chronic blood loss: the most common cause in adults, from the gastrointestinal tract or from menstrual periods.
- Dietary factors: a vegan diet, drinking tea, calcium antacids, and medications, particularly proton pump inhibitors.
- Malabsorption: gastric bypass surgery, celiac sprue and food allergies.
- Increased demand: pregnancy, and growth in infancy or adolescence.

A quick way to hold this together: iron deficiency happens when iron is lost, not taken in, not absorbed, or needed in larger amounts than usual.

cards.t: Who gets iron deficiency anemia
q: how common is iron deficiency anemia
who is most at risk for iron deficiency
why are women of childbearing age at risk of iron deficiency
cards.x:
Iron deficiency is the cause of 50% of anemia worldwide and of almost 1 million deaths a year. Most of those deaths, 71%, are in Africa and Asia, and only 1.4% are in North America. Rates are higher in developing countries than in the United States.

Within the United States the risk is not even:

- Men under 50: about 1%.
- Women of childbearing age: about 10%, because of menstrual losses.
- Children aged 12 to 36 months: 9% are iron deficient, and one third of them develop anemia.
- Low-income families are particularly at risk.

The pattern follows the causes: groups that lose blood regularly or are growing fast are the ones who run short.

cards.t: Signs and symptoms of iron deficiency anemia
q: what are the symptoms of iron deficiency anemia
what are spoon-shaped nails
what is pica
what nail change goes with iron deficiency
cards.x:
Iron deficiency causes the general symptoms of any anemia: fatigue, pallor, decreased exercise tolerance, and shortness of breath, especially with exertion.

Some findings are more specific to iron deficiency:

- A smooth tongue.
- Pica, which is the urge to eat things that are not food. It is common.
- Koilonychia: nail bed changes where the nail turns up at the edge into a flat, concave, spoon-shaped nail.
- Cheilosis.
- Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

Koilonychia, cheilosis and Plummer-Vinson syndrome are the ones starred as worth remembering.

cards.t: Diagnosing iron deficiency anemia
q: how do you diagnose iron deficiency anemia
what labs show iron deficiency
what does the smear look like in iron deficiency
what extra tests do you order in iron deficiency
cards.x:
Iron deficiency shows up in three places.

- Complete blood count: microcytosis, meaning the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is below 80 femtoliters, and hypochromia, meaning a low mean corpuscular hemoglobin, which looks like pale red cells on the stained smear.
- Iron panel: reduced serum ferritin, reduced transferrin saturation, and increased total iron-binding capacity.
- Peripheral smear: microcytic, hypochromic red cells.

Small, pale cells with low ferritin, low saturation and a high binding capacity is the picture to know.

Because the cause matters, additional tests are a urinalysis and a fecal occult blood test (stool guaiac) to look for a gastrointestinal bleed, and you can consider coagulation studies (prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time).

cards.t: Why a normal ferritin does not rule out iron deficiency
q: why can ferritin be normal in iron deficiency
what is an acute phase reactant
can you have iron deficiency with a high ferritin
cards.x:
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant. That means it rises with inflammation, and transferrin does too, to a lesser degree. So a patient with an inflammatory condition, such as an infection or an autoimmune disease, who is also iron deficient may have a normal or even elevated ferritin.

The takeaway is that a normal or elevated ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency anemia. If that is a concern, consider an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-reactive protein (CRP), which help show whether inflammation is present.

The same rule comes back with iron overload: ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so read it with the whole lab picture.

cards.t: What else looks like iron deficiency: the microcytic differential
q: what is on the differential for iron deficiency anemia
how do you tell thalassemia from iron deficiency
how do you tell anemia of chronic disease from iron deficiency
cards.x:
Other small-cell anemias can look like iron deficiency, so the differential includes:

- Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation): ferritin is normal or increased, and the total iron-binding capacity is not high the way it is in iron deficiency.
- Thalassemia: more microcytosis than you would expect for the hemoglobin level. Unlike most other anemias, the red cell count is normal or elevated. The smear resembles severe iron deficiency.
- Lead poisoning.
- Zinc deficiency, which is only listed.
- Sideroblastic anemia.

Each of these has its own tell: the iron panel for anemia of chronic disease, the red cell count for thalassemia, the lead exposure and basophilic stippling for lead poisoning, and ring sideroblasts on the marrow for sideroblastic anemia.

cards.t: Iron deficiency anemia: the overview
q: what is iron deficiency anemia
what labs show iron deficiency anemia
what should I look for in an adult with iron deficiency
cards.x:
Iron deficiency anemia is anemia from too little iron. It is the cause of 50% of anemia worldwide. The red cells come out small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic), because there is not enough iron to build hemoglobin.

The iron panel is the giveaway: low ferritin (the iron storage protein), low transferrin saturation, and a high total iron-binding capacity. Think of the high binding capacity as the body holding out more empty seats for iron because there is so little of it around.

In an adult, look for chronic blood loss, which is the most common cause. Treatment is to replace the iron and still correct the underlying cause.

cards.t: Treating the cause of iron deficiency
k: work up the source of blood loss
q: how do you treat iron deficiency anemia
why do you scope a patient with iron deficiency
when should you stop anticoagulants in iron deficiency
cards.x:
Treatment starts with fixing the reason the iron was lost, then replacing the iron.

- Menstrual blood loss: an oral contraceptive, and consider a continuous-cycle one.
- Gastrointestinal bleed: a gastroenterology consult for colonoscopy or endoscopy, which evaluates for colorectal cancer.
- Anticoagulants: discontinue them if the anemia is severe, and consult cardiology.
- Then iron replacement.

Refer to hematology if the diagnosis is not confirmed or the patient does not respond to oral iron.

Replacing iron alone without finding the source would just refill a leaking bucket.

cards.t: Oral iron: ferrous sulfate, side effects and better dosing
q: how is iron deficiency treated with pills
why does oral iron cause constipation
is alternate-day iron better
why take iron with orange juice
cards.x:
Oral iron salts, such as ferrous sulfate, are one way to replace iron, given once daily or every other day. They are poorly absorbed, cause lots of side effects, and adherence is poor ("people hate it"). Gastrointestinal side effects are common, especially nausea and constipation, so always give an as-needed laxative or stool softener with it. Taking it with food reduces side effects but also decreases absorption.

Two ways to do better:

- Less frequent dosing: studies show better absorption and fewer side effects, and alternate-day dosing is probably best, although adherence can be a problem.
- A ferrous sulfate preparation (44 mg per 5 mL, as elemental iron) once daily in the morning, on an empty stomach, with a full glass of orange juice. The low pH, citric acid and vitamin C help uptake and limit how much free iron reaches the rest of the gut, so there are fewer side effects.

cards.t: How long to treat iron deficiency and when to use parenteral iron
q: how long should iron be continued
what is the expected response to iron therapy
when do you use parenteral iron
cards.x:
An appropriate response to iron is the hematocrit moving halfway back toward normal within 3 weeks and back to baseline after 2 months.

Do not stop when the counts look normal. Continue the iron for 3 to 6 months after the counts normalize, to replenish the iron stores.

Parenteral iron (given by injection or infusion rather than by mouth) is for patients who cannot tolerate oral iron or who are refractory to it. If the diagnosis is not confirmed or the patient is unresponsive to oral iron, refer to hematology.

Usually the anemia resolves once the cause and the iron stores are corrected.

cards.t: Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation): what and why
q: what is anemia of chronic disease
why does inflammation cause anemia
what does hepcidin do
who gets anemia of chronic disease
cards.x:
Anemia of chronic disease, also called anemia of chronic inflammation, is anemia caused by any inflammatory condition: infection, autoimmune disease or a neoplasm. It initially resembles iron deficiency anemia.

The cause is multifactorial:

- Inflammatory cytokines, in particular interleukin-6, upregulate hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption. Interleukin-6 raises hepcidin, which locks iron away.
- Systemic inflammation inhibits the kidney's production of erythropoietin.
- There is likely also direct suppression of the bone marrow by inflammation.

It is the second most common anemia and can occur at any age. Older adults are at increased risk because they have more chronic inflammatory disease; about 1 million people older than 65 in the United States have it. Its signs and symptoms are similar to iron deficiency anemia and resemble the causative condition.

cards.t: Anemia of chronic disease labs compared with iron deficiency
k: ferritin in anemia of chronic disease
TIBC in anemia of chronic disease
q: how do you tell anemia of chronic disease from iron deficiency
what is the ferritin in anemia of chronic disease
what does a ferritin under 30 mean in chronic disease
cards.x:
Anemia of chronic disease is worked up with the same labs as iron deficiency anemia. If inflammation is not clinically known, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-reactive protein (CRP) can help.

The key contrast is in the iron stores and binding capacity. In iron deficiency the ferritin is low and the total iron-binding capacity is increased. In anemia of chronic disease the ferritin is normal or increased, and the total iron-binding capacity is not raised. The mean corpuscular volume is normal or low, and the reticulocytes are usually decreased.

The serum iron is not a safe thing to lean on here, so go by the ferritin and the binding capacity.

One more rule: a ferritin less than 30 ng/mL (67 pmol/L) indicates coexistent iron deficiency, meaning the patient has both problems.

cards.t: Treating anemia of chronic disease
k: erythropoietin for anemia of chronic disease
q: how do you treat anemia of chronic disease
when is erythropoietin used in anemia of chronic disease
does anemia of chronic disease need a hematology referral
cards.x:
The most important treatment is to treat the underlying condition. The anemia can persist while the underlying disease is active.

Some patients may benefit from erythropoietin supplementation (epoetin alfa, Procrit). Its Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved indications are a hemoglobin less than 10 g/dL, and anemia due to rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatitis C, zidovudine therapy in patients with human immunodeficiency virus, myelosuppressive chemotherapy of a solid malignancy, or chronic kidney disease. Some patients may need parenteral iron. A referral to hematology is not usually needed.

cards.t: Hepcidin and interleukin-6: why inflammation locks iron away
k: why is iron blocked in inflammation
q: what does hepcidin do
how does interleukin-6 cause anemia
why does inflammation lower iron absorption
what is the link between hepcidin and anemia of chronic disease
cards.x:
Hepcidin is the hormone that blocks iron absorption, and inflammation turns it up. Inflammatory cytokines, in particular interleukin-6, upregulate hepcidin. Interleukin-6 raises hepcidin, which locks iron away, so the body has iron on hand but cannot use it to build red cells.

This is the main mechanism to know for anemia of chronic disease (anemia of chronic inflammation). Two other things happen alongside it: systemic inflammation inhibits the kidney's production of erythropoietin, and there is likely direct suppression of the bone marrow.

Hepcidin also turns up in two other places in this unit. In anemia of chronic kidney disease, inflammation and hepcidin restrict the available iron. In sideroblastic anemia, the modern classification names dyserythropoiesis, that is, hypohepcidinemia, meaning low hepcidin.

cards.t: Sideroblastic anemia and ring sideroblasts
q: what is sideroblastic anemia
what is a ring sideroblast
why does sideroblastic anemia have high iron
cards.x:
Sideroblastic anemia is an anemia of red cell precursors in which iron-containing mitochondria form a basophilic ring around the nucleus. These are ring sideroblasts, seen on a bone marrow aspirate, and they are the defining feature.

It is an iron overload picture, not an iron shortage: total body iron is in excess, and the serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin are all increased. That is the opposite of iron deficiency anemia, even though the cells may be small.

It is rare. About two thirds of cases present in males in early childhood or adolescence and one third in young to middle-aged females, but it can occur at any age.

cards.t: Types and causes of sideroblastic anemia
q: what causes sideroblastic anemia
what are the three types of sideroblastic anemia
which drugs cause sideroblastic anemia
cards.x:
There are three types.

- Hereditary: usually X-linked.
- Acquired: usually with myelodysplastic syndrome.
- Acquired and reversible: alcohol, certain drugs (isoniazid and chlorambucil), copper deficiency, hypothermia and lead poisoning.

The modern classification groups them by mechanism: dyserythropoiesis (that is, hypohepcidinemia) and transfusion dependence (myelodysplastic syndrome and thalassemia).

For the reversible group, removing the cause is the treatment.

cards.t: Presentation and diagnosis of sideroblastic anemia
q: how do you diagnose sideroblastic anemia
what does the smear look like in sideroblastic anemia
how severe is sideroblastic anemia
cards.x:
There are no specific clinical features other than those of anemia. The anemia is usually moderate, with a hematocrit of 20 to 30%.

On the blood tests, the cells show variable microcytosis and hypochromia, and the smear is dimorphic, meaning it has microcytes, normal cells and macrocytes together. The iron studies show excess iron: increased serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin. If the cause is copper deficiency, the zinc level is increased.

The defining finding is ring sideroblasts on a bone marrow aspirate.

cards.t: Treating sideroblastic anemia
q: how do you treat sideroblastic anemia
does erythropoietin work in sideroblastic anemia
what is luspatercept used for
cards.x:
If the anemia is acquired, remove the offending agent. Red cell transfusion is given if the anemia is severe.

Other options are limited. The response to recombinant erythropoietin is typically poor. Some patients respond occasionally to oral pyridoxine. Luspatercept was recently approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for myelodysplastic syndrome with ringed sideroblasts.

Refer to hematology if diagnostic or transfusion support is needed. The outlook is variable, and clonal forms may need continued follow-up.

cards.t: Lead poisoning: anemia, basophilic stippling and sources
q: what is lead poisoning anemia
what is basophilic stippling
what are sources of lead exposure
cards.x:
Lead poisoning (plumbism) is lead toxicity that causes a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. On the smear, look for basophilic stippling, an abnormal collection of nucleic acids in the cells.

Sources of exposure include industrial exposure, gasoline sniffing, lodged bullets, cooking utensils containing lead, lead-based paint chips, and contaminated water, as in the Flint water crisis.

It also shows up elsewhere in this unit: lead poisoning is on the differential of iron deficiency anemia because of the small, pale cells, and it is one of the reversible causes of sideroblastic anemia.

cards.t: Lead poisoning: symptoms and treatment
q: what are the symptoms of lead poisoning
what is a lead line
how do you treat lead poisoning
cards.x:
The neurologic system is the most vulnerable: irritability, behavioral changes and peripheral neuropathy. The gastrointestinal symptoms are abdominal colic, nausea and constipation, and occasionally diarrhea. There may be a lead line in the gums, a dark band along the gum margin above the teeth.

Treatment is to stop the exposure. Further treatment is based on the lead level. In severe cases with neurologic effects, give chelating agents (drugs that bind the lead): succimer (Chemet), dimercaprol, or ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).

Pair the two findings in your head: a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling plus neurologic and gut symptoms points to lead.

cards.t: Macrocytic anemia: megaloblastic versus non-megaloblastic
q: what is macrocytic anemia
what causes macrocytic anemia
what is the difference between megaloblastic and non-megaloblastic macrocytosis
cards.x:
Macrocytic anemia is anemia with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) above 100 femtoliters. It splits into two categories.

- Megaloblastic anemia: caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency or folate deficiency.
- Non-megaloblastic anemia: alcohol (common) or a drug, hypothyroidism, liver failure, or bone marrow dysplasia.

The non-megaloblastic causes usually have an MCV below 115 femtoliters.

cards.t: Megaloblastic anemia: megaloblasts and the lab pattern
q: what is megaloblastic anemia
what do megaloblasts look like
why do hypersegmented neutrophils appear
what is the red cell distribution width in megaloblastic anemia
cards.x:
Megaloblastic anemia is a macrocytic anemia with megaloblasts, which are early red cell precursors. The blood smear shows macrocytosis with macro-ovalocytes (large oval red cells) and hypersegmented neutrophils.

The underlying problem is impaired DNA synthesis. That causes nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and impaired hematopoiesis. Other myeloid cells, the granulocytes and megakaryocytes, are affected to a lesser degree.

On the complete blood count, the red cells, hemoglobin and hematocrit are decreased and the mean corpuscular volume is increased. The mean corpuscular hemoglobin and its concentration are normal to slightly increased. The red cell distribution width is increased, which reflects anisocytosis (cells of unequal size). Reticulocytes vary.

cards.t: How vitamin B12 is absorbed
q: how is vitamin B12 absorbed
what does intrinsic factor do
where is B12 absorbed
how long do B12 stores last
cards.x:
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) travels through a chain of steps, and breaking any link causes deficiency.

1. Peptic digestion in the stomach releases dietary B12.
2. Parietal cells in the gastric mucosa release intrinsic factor, which binds the free B12 and protects it from digestive enzymes.
3. The B12-intrinsic factor complex passes to the distal ileum and binds cubilin, the intrinsic factor receptor.
4. Absorbed B12 binds transcobalamin and is stored in the liver.

Normal liver stores last about 3 to 4 years or more, so deficiency is slow to appear.

cards.t: Pernicious anemia
k: most common cause of B12 deficiency
q: what is pernicious anemia
what is the most common cause of B12 deficiency
why does pernicious anemia raise the risk of stomach cancer
cards.x:
Pernicious anemia is the most frequent cause of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. It is an autoimmune reaction against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor. Since parietal cells make intrinsic factor, losing them means B12 cannot be absorbed.

The autoimmune attack also causes gastric atrophy (a thinned-out stomach lining) and an increased risk of gastric cancer. The result is a megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia from too little B12.

cards.t: Neurologic and other features of B12 deficiency
q: what are the symptoms of B12 deficiency
why does B12 deficiency cause neurologic problems
what is stocking and glove numbness
what is glossitis
cards.x:
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes the findings of all anemias: fatigue, pallor and headache, with dyspnea and heart failure when severe. There are gastrointestinal findings too: glossitis (a smooth, red tongue) and oral ulcers.

The distinguishing finding is neurologic, from demyelination, especially of the dorsal and lateral spinal cord tracts.

- Neuropsychiatric changes: depression, irritability, insomnia, cognitive slowing, dementia.
- Symmetric numbness, tingling and burning in the hands and feet, called a stocking and glove distribution.
- Later, an unsteady gait and loss of position sense.

The neurologic findings may or may not improve with B12.

cards.t: Homocysteine versus methylmalonic acid: B12 versus folate
k: how to tell B12 from folate deficiency
q: how do you tell B12 deficiency from folate deficiency
why is methylmalonic acid elevated in B12 deficiency
which labs rise in folate deficiency
cards.x:
For any macrocytic anemia, the first tests are vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate levels, which are not very sensitive, plus a peripheral blood smear. If the result is borderline or suspicion continues, add two more levels.

- Homocysteine: converting homocysteine to methionine needs both B12 and folate, so it rises in either deficiency.
- Methylmalonic acid: converting L-methylmalonyl CoA to succinyl CoA needs only B12, so methylmalonic acid is elevated in B12 deficiency but not in folate deficiency.

So B12 deficiency has both elevated, while folate deficiency has an elevated homocysteine and a normal methylmalonic acid. Methylmalonic acid is the one that points to B12 alone.

cards.t: Testing for pernicious anemia
q: what tests confirm pernicious anemia
how specific are anti-intrinsic factor antibodies
how is pernicious anemia usually diagnosed in practice
cards.x:
Three tests are used when pernicious anemia is suspected.

- Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies: specific but not sensitive.
- Anti-parietal cell antibodies: neither sensitive nor specific.
- Gastric biopsy: may show chronic atrophic gastritis.

In reality, the normal diagnostic pathway is a megaloblastic picture that corrects with vitamin B12 (cobalamin), which is why a trial of parenteral B12 is on the list of tests.

Specific but not sensitive means a positive result is useful, but a negative one does not rule it out.

cards.t: Folate deficiency
q: what is folate deficiency
what causes folate deficiency
how do you tell folate deficiency from B12 deficiency
cards.x:
Folate deficiency is a megaloblastic anemia from lack of folate. Its causes are:

- Diet: the impoverished or indigent, people with alcohol use disorder, and the elderly.
- Increased demand: pregnancy.
- Impaired absorption: in the proximal small bowel.
- Drugs: methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, phenytoin and metformin.

The labs show a mean corpuscular volume above 100 femtoliters with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, a folate level to check, an elevated homocysteine, and a methylmalonic acid that is not elevated.

The neurologic findings are what distinguish vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, not folate deficiency.

cards.t: Check for B12 deficiency before giving folate
q: why check B12 before giving folic acid
how is B12 deficiency treated
how is folate deficiency treated
cards.x:
Before replacing folate, evaluate for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. If you give folate to an unrecognized B12 deficiency, the labs may improve while permanent neurologic symptoms worsen, because the neurologic damage keeps progressing.

Replacement for each deficiency:

- B12 deficiency: B12 injections (subcutaneously or intramuscularly) weekly for 3 weeks, or oral cobalamin daily.
- Folate deficiency: folic acid by mouth or parenterally daily for 1 to 2 weeks.

Do not skip the B12 check: it is what protects the nerves.

cards.t: Which tests go with which anemia
q: what labs do I order for microcytic anemia
what tests do I order for macrocytic anemia
which tests for suspected pernicious anemia
cards.x:
The tests build up in layers.

- Every anemia: complete blood count, reticulocyte count, and the calculated reticulocyte index.
- Microcytic anemia (small cells): serum iron, transferrin saturation, total iron-binding capacity and serum ferritin, plus a fecal occult blood test and a urinalysis.
- Macrocytic anemia (large cells): vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate levels, review of the peripheral smear, and then homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.
- If pernicious anemia is suspected: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies, and a trial of parenteral B12 (B12 given by injection).

Match the test to the cell size first, and the extra tests only come in when the first ones leave a question.

cards.t: Anemia of chronic kidney disease: mechanism and labs
q: what is anemia of chronic kidney disease
why does kidney disease cause anemia
what do the labs look like in anemia of chronic kidney disease
cards.x:
Anemia of chronic kidney disease is extremely common. Its incidence rises as the glomerular filtration rate falls, and it is almost universal in dialysis patients. It is primarily, but not completely, due to decreased erythropoietin, so the erythropoietin response is inappropriately low. Inflammation and hepcidin also restrict the available iron.

The cells are normocytic: the mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin and its concentration are normal. The red cell distribution width is increased, and the reticulocytes are decreased. So the picture is a normocytic anemia with low reticulocytes in a patient with a falling filtration rate or on dialysis.

cards.t: Workup and treatment of anemia of chronic kidney disease
q: how do you treat anemia of chronic kidney disease
what does a low transferrin saturation with a normal ferritin mean in kidney disease
what is Triferic
cards.x:
Order a complete blood count, a reticulocyte count, ferritin and transferrin saturation, and assess other causes of anemia. A low transferrin saturation may indicate iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite a normal or high ferritin, meaning the marrow cannot get enough iron even though the stores look fine.

For treatment, correct iron deficiency. Consider oral or intravenous iron and an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, depending on the chronic kidney disease stage, hemoglobin and risk. Ferric pyrophosphate citrate (Triferic) is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved additive to the dialysate that replaces the 5 to 7 mg of iron lost in each hemodialysis treatment.

Follow up by monitoring hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure, with nephrology for advanced disease, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent decisions or uncertainty. The anemia is often chronic and may improve with iron or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent.

cards.t: Erythropoietin in anemia of chronic kidney disease and chronic disease
q: why does kidney disease cause low erythropoietin anemia
when is erythropoietin used
which anemias respond to erythropoietin
cards.x:
Erythropoietin is the signal that drives red cell production, and several anemias in this unit come down to too little of it, or too little response to it.

- Chronic kidney disease: the anemia is primarily, but not completely, from decreased erythropoietin, so the response is inappropriately low. Inflammation and hepcidin restrict the available iron as well.
- Anemia of chronic disease: systemic inflammation inhibits the kidney's erythropoietin production. Erythropoietin supplementation (epoetin alfa) may benefit some patients, and treating the underlying condition is still the most important step.
- Sideroblastic anemia: the response to recombinant erythropoietin is typically poor.

For anemia of chronic kidney disease, consider an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) based on the stage of kidney disease, the hemoglobin and the risk.

cards.t: Aplastic anemia: pancytopenia from lost stem cells
q: what is aplastic anemia
why does aplastic anemia cause infections and bleeding
who gets aplastic anemia
how is aplastic anemia diagnosed
cards.x:
Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia: loss of all three cell lines, the red cells, platelets and white cells. The defining feature is loss of hematopoietic stem cells, the marrow cells that make the blood cells.

So the symptoms come in three groups: recurrent infections (from low neutrophils), bleeding, petechiae and purpura (from low platelets), and fatigue and pallor (from anemia).

Half of cases occur in the first three decades of life, with a small peak in childhood and a second small peak at ages 20 to 25. The male-to-female ratio is about 1:1, and it affects 0.6 to 6.1 cases per million.

A bone marrow biopsy is required for the diagnosis and to exclude other causes.

cards.t: Causes and associations of aplastic anemia
q: what causes aplastic anemia
what drugs cause aplastic anemia
how do drugs and viruses cause aplastic anemia
cards.x:
The pathophysiology has four routes: autoimmune destruction, direct injury to the hematopoietic stem cells (drugs, chemicals, radiation), viral infections, and genetic causes. Drugs, chemicals, viruses or mutations can alter the stem cells and predispose them to autoimmune destruction.

Associations to know:

- Cytotoxic or chemotherapeutic drugs, but it is not called aplastic anemia if the marrow loss is an expected effect of the drug.
- Chloramphenicol.
- Ionizing radiation.
- Toxins: benzene and pesticides.
- Clonal abnormalities: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia.
- Inherited: Fanconi anemia, diagnosed in childhood, and other rare conditions.

cards.t: Treatment and outlook of aplastic anemia
q: how is aplastic anemia treated
what is the prognosis of aplastic anemia
what precautions does an aplastic anemia patient need
cards.x:
Aplastic anemia needs urgent or emergent consultation with a hematologist/oncologist. The treatment is bone marrow transplant, and the patient needs infection and bleeding precautions because the infection-fighting cells and the platelets are both low.

The outlook depends on severity and response to treatment. Five-year survival is above 75% after a bone marrow transplant from a suitable donor. The majority of untreated patients die within one year.

cards.t: Leukopenia and neutropenia: calculating and grading the neutrophil count
q: what is neutropenia
how do you calculate the absolute neutrophil count
what counts as severe neutropenia
cards.x:
Leukopenia is a low total white blood cell count. Neutropenia is defined by the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), which you calculate:

ANC = white blood cell count x (neutrophils + bands)% / 100

The grades are:

- Mild: 1,000 to 1,500 cells/microliter.
- Moderate: 500 to 999.
- Severe: below 500.

Common causes are viral illness, medications or chemotherapy, autoimmune disease, nutrient deficits, and marrow pathology.

To work it up, repeat the complete blood count with differential, review the trend and the peripheral smear, and check the other cell lines. Escalate to hematology for persistent or unexplained severe neutropenia, other cytopenias or an abnormal smear.

cards.t: Fever with a low neutrophil count: the emergency
q: why is fever with neutropenia an emergency
what do you do for fever with an absolute neutrophil count under 500
why might a neutropenic patient look well
cards.x:
Infection risk is predicted by the severity and duration of the neutropenia and by the patient's immune status. Profound neutropenia may have subtle findings, so an infection can look quiet.

That is why fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 500, or expected to fall below 500, is an emergency. The patient needs prompt assessment: vitals, a targeted examination for a source, and cultures. Start empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics without delay. Educate the patient to report fever or rigors promptly.

cards.t: Managing chronic neutropenia and its outlook
q: how do you manage chronic neutropenia
when is granulocyte colony-stimulating factor used
does neutropenia go away
cards.x:
For chronic neutropenia, stop an offending drug when appropriate and correct deficiencies. Selected patients need granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Monitor the counts, and send marrow disorders to a specialist.

The outlook depends on the cause. Transient viral leukopenia often resolves after recovery, and reversible causes often resolve. Persistent or severe neutropenia carries greater infection risk and may indicate marrow disease.

cards.t: Hemolytic anemia: what they all share
q: what is hemolytic anemia
what do all hemolytic anemias have in common
what is the first clue to hemolysis
cards.x:
Hemolysis is shortened survival of circulating red cells because they are destroyed prematurely. There are many causes, mild to severe and acute to chronic. An unexpected rise in the reticulocyte count, even without anemia or symptoms, should prompt consideration of hemolysis.

All hemolytic anemias share three things:

- A decreased red cell life span.
- A compensatory increase in red cell production.
- Retention of the products of red cell destruction, including iron.

Those lead to marrow hyperplasia and increased reticulocytes. In severe chronic hemolysis, red cells are made outside the marrow in the liver, spleen and lymph nodes (extramedullary hematopoiesis).

cards.t: What keeps a red cell alive in the circulation
q: why do red cells survive squeezing through capillaries
what does the red cell cytoskeleton do
why is the red cell a biconcave disc
cards.x:
A red cell, about 6 micrometers across, has to squeeze through capillaries of about 2 micrometers. Three features let it survive that shear stress.

- A highly deformable membrane and cytoskeleton. The cytoskeletal proteins are spectrin and ankyrin.
- A strong redox environment that prevents oxidative stress.
- An optimal surface-to-volume ratio: the biconcave disc has about 40% more surface area than a sphere.

Hemolysis occurs when the cell can no longer withstand this. So hemolysis can follow when any of these protections fails: the membrane, the redox protection, or the shape.

cards.t: Causes of hemolysis: intracorpuscular versus extracorpuscular
q: what causes hemolytic anemia
what is the difference between intracorpuscular and extracorpuscular hemolysis
which hemolytic anemias are genetic
cards.x:
Hemolysis causes are split by where the problem sits.

Intracorpuscular defects are intrinsic to the red cell itself:

- Hemoglobinopathies: sickle cell disease, thalassemia, unstable hemoglobin variants.
- Membrane and cytoskeletal defects: hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, stomatocytosis.
- Metabolic abnormalities: glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency and pyruvate kinase deficiency.

Extracorpuscular defects come from outside the cell:

- Immune-mediated: autoimmune hemolytic anemia and transfusion reactions.
- Hypersplenism.
- Mechanical trauma (shear stress).
- Oxidative stress: G6PD deficiency and methemoglobinemia.
- Infection: malaria, babesiosis.
- Toxins: snake and insect bites, burns, copper poisoning.

The genetic causes are defects in the red cell membrane, the hemoglobin itself, or enzymes.

cards.t: Spherocytes and genetic causes of hemolysis
q: what do spherocytes look like
what are the genetic causes of hemolytic anemia
what is hereditary spherocytosis
cards.x:
The genetic causes of hemolysis are defects in the red cell membrane, in the hemoglobin itself, or in enzymes. On a smear, spherocytes are small round red cells without the central pallor (the pale middle) that normal biconcave cells have.

Membrane and cytoskeletal defects, which sit among the intracorpuscular causes, include hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis and stomatocytosis. A red cell has to squeeze through capillaries much narrower than itself, and a highly deformable membrane and cytoskeleton, with the proteins spectrin and ankyrin, is part of what lets it survive that.

The other genetic groups are the hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease, thalassemia, unstable hemoglobin variants) and the enzyme problems (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase deficiencies).

cards.t: Extravascular versus intravascular hemolysis
q: what is the difference between extravascular and intravascular hemolysis
why does haptoglobin fall in hemolysis
why does intravascular hemolysis cause hemoglobin in the urine
cards.x:
When a red cell is destroyed, its contents are released, and the main concern is hemoglobin.

- Extravascular hemolysis is the more common way. It happens mainly in the spleen and liver, where macrophages engulf the red cells and release unconjugated bilirubin, which the liver then conjugates.
- Intravascular hemolysis happens inside the blood vessels. Free hemoglobin is picked up by haptoglobin and taken to the liver. This is incomplete, so some hemoglobin appears in the urine.

Haptoglobin is the carrier that picks up the free hemoglobin, which is why it is decreased or absent in intravascular hemolysis.

cards.t: Lab workup for hemolysis: bilirubin, haptoglobin, LDH and schistocytes
q: what labs do you order for suspected hemolysis
what is the hallmark smear finding of hemolysis
when does jaundice appear in hemolysis
cards.x:
The workup for suspected hemolytic anemia is a complete blood count, reticulocyte count, serum bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), haptoglobin, urinalysis and a peripheral smear review.

- Bilirubin: both conjugated and unconjugated are likely elevated, with unconjugated greater than conjugated. Clinical jaundice appears when total bilirubin exceeds 2.0 mg/dL (normal 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL).
- Haptoglobin: decreased or absent with intravascular hemolysis.
- Lactate dehydrogenase: a common cytoplasmic enzyme, elevated with any cell lysis.
- Smear: order one on any patient with suspected hemolysis. The hallmark finding is schistocytes, which are red blood cell fragments.

cards.t: How hemolysis presents
q: what are the symptoms of hemolytic anemia
what findings point to hemolysis rather than another anemia
what is often the first sign of hemolysis
cards.x:
Patients have the typical anemia symptoms: fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain and pallor. In severe cases there can be chest pain, high-output cardiac failure and shock.

The differentiating findings, the ones that point to hemolysis, are jaundice, splenomegaly, joint pain and hematuria. Often the first indication is an increase in the reticulocyte count.

cards.t: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: what it is and what causes it
q: what is autoimmune hemolytic anemia
what causes autoimmune hemolytic anemia
is autoimmune hemolytic anemia always primary
cards.x:
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is hemolysis caused by an antibody against the red cell membrane. The immune system tags its own red cells for destruction. It may be primary, with de novo antibody production, or secondary. Primary autoimmune hemolytic anemia is almost always immunoglobulin G (IgG). A transfusion reaction is an example of this kind of immune-mediated hemolysis.

Common secondary causes:

- Viruses: human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).
- Autoimmune disorders: lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ulcerative colitis.
- Lymphoproliferative disorders: leukemias and lymphomas, multiple myeloma.
- Pregnancy.

cards.t: The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
q: what is the Coombs test
how does the direct antiglobulin test work
what does a positive Coombs test mean
cards.x:
The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), also called the Coombs test, shows whether a patient's red cells are coated with antibody. The patient's red cells are washed and combined with Coombs reagent. The reagent antibodies bind only cells coated with IgG or complement. If the test is positive, they cross-link the cells, and the red cells agglutinate (clump).

So a positive test means IgG or complement is sitting on the patient's red cells, which is the finding that goes with autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

cards.t: Venous thromboembolism risk in autoimmune hemolytic anemia
q: why is autoimmune hemolytic anemia associated with blood clots
what should you check for in autoimmune hemolytic anemia
does autoimmune hemolytic anemia need clot prophylaxis
cards.x:
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Keep it in mind with signs of a deep vein thrombosis, and consider a D-dimer and bilateral leg ultrasound for deep vein thrombosis and/or pulmonary embolism.

Give venous thromboembolism prophylaxis to inpatients, and consider it in outpatients.

cards.t: Treating autoimmune hemolytic anemia
q: how do you treat autoimmune hemolytic anemia
when is autoimmune hemolytic anemia an emergency
what is rituximab used for in hemolysis
cards.x:
First stabilize if the hemoglobin is below 6, the decline is rapid, or the patient is unstable. Contact the blood bank, because compatible blood must be found. Rule out secondary causes.

Treat with glucocorticoids initially. Rituximab (Rituxan), an antibody against cluster of differentiation 20 (CD20), is also used. Other options are immunosuppressants and splenectomy.

Relapse may occur, and the outcome depends on the cause and the response.

cards.t: G6PD deficiency: what it is and who gets it
q: what is G6PD deficiency
why are mostly men affected by G6PD deficiency
which populations have the most G6PD deficiency
cards.x:
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is the most common genetic disorder of red cells, affecting 200 to 400 million people. The missing enzyme protects red cells against oxidative damage, so exposure to oxidative stress causes an acute hemolytic anemia. It is usually triggered by drugs with high oxidative potential.

It is X-linked recessive, so generally only males are affected. Carrier females have two red cell populations, one normal and one deficient, and are generally unaffected.

It varies by population. It is highest in Kurdish Jews (60 to 70%), Sardinians (4 to 35%, by village), Nigerians (22%) and Thai people (17%), and about 11 to 12% of American Black people have it. It is 0 to 1% in Japanese and Koreans.

cards.t: Why G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis: Heinz bodies and bite cells
q: what are Heinz bodies
what are bite cells
how does G6PD deficiency cause hemolysis
cards.x:
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is needed in the glutathione pathway. Without reduced glutathione, the red cell is more susceptible to oxidative damage.

Under oxidative stress, Heinz bodies form inside the red cell. They show as small dark dots on a supravital stain. Splenic macrophages then remove them by taking a chunk out of the cell, which leaves a bite cell. The result is both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

So Heinz bodies are the damage inside the cell, and bite cells are what is left after the spleen picks that damage out.

cards.t: Triggers of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
q: what triggers hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
which drugs should people with G6PD deficiency avoid
do fava beans cause hemolysis
cards.x:
The common triggers are things with high oxidative potential:

- Fava beans.
- Naphthalene (mothballs).
- Nitrofurantoin.
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim).
- Methylene blue.
- Phenazopyridine.
- Quinolones.

Some antimalarials can trigger hemolysis, but they do not all carry the same risk, so do not assume every antimalarial is a trigger.

The treatment follows directly: avoid the trigger.

cards.t: Presentation and diagnosis of G6PD deficiency
q: what are the symptoms of a G6PD hemolytic attack
when do you test for G6PD deficiency
why test for G6PD weeks after an attack
cards.x:
With glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, there are no symptoms until the patient is exposed to oxidative stress. Drug-induced hemolysis is acute, of variable severity, and comes after a lag of 2 to 3 days. Symptoms are abdominal pain, jaundice and dark urine, and the exam may show splenomegaly.

The labs are consistent with hemolytic anemia. During an attack the smear may show Heinz bodies and bite cells. The diagnosis is confirmed by a low G6PD level roughly 8 weeks after an attack, not during one.

cards.t: Treating G6PD deficiency and its outlook
q: how do you treat G6PD deficiency
does G6PD deficiency need a splenectomy
what should a patient with G6PD deficiency be told
cards.x:
The treatment is "don't eat that": avoid the trigger. Hydrate, and transfuse if needed. Splenectomy is considered only for recurrent attacks.

Education matters: avoid oxidative triggers, and seek care for jaundice or dark urine. The outlook is usually favorable with trigger avoidance.

cards.t: Thalassemia: what goes wrong with the globin chains
q: what is thalassemia
why does thalassemia cause hemolysis
what is the difference between alpha and beta thalassemia
cards.x:
Thalassemia is a hemoglobinopathy from mutations that cause deficient synthesis of alpha or beta globins, the building blocks of hemoglobin. There is a deficiency of hemoglobin, and most erythroblasts die in the marrow.

The main problem is the imbalance in expression. The globin subunits that are made in excess accumulate and precipitate, which causes red cell destruction in the spleen.

cards.t: Thalassemia genetics: how many genes are mutated
q: how do the number of mutated genes change thalassemia severity
what is the alpha thalassemia 1 trait
what is a silent carrier
cards.x:
There are 4 alpha globin genes and 2 beta globin genes, and they are inherited. The phenotype depends on how many are mutated, from a silent carrier (one alpha gene lost) to a form incompatible with life.

Alpha thalassemia is prevalent in Southern China, Malaysia, Thailand and the Mediterranean region, with mild forms in people of African origin. Asian ancestry often carries the alpha thalassemia 1 trait, with both deletions on one side, and has a higher risk of hydrops fetalis. African ancestry more often carries the alpha thalassemia 2 trait, with one deletion on each side.

With a family history, preconception testing and counseling are available.

cards.t: Clinical features and lab testing in thalassemia
q: what are the signs of thalassemia
how do you diagnose thalassemia
what does hemoglobin electrophoresis show
cards.x:
The course varies with the mutation. Features include varying degrees of hemolytic anemia, iron overload, splenomegaly, extramedullary hematopoiesis, jaundice, and skeletal changes such as a prominent forehead and an overgrown upper jaw.

The labs generally show decreased hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and a Coombs-negative picture, so the hemolysis is not immune-mediated. For a given hemoglobin, the microcytosis is greater than expected, with a normal or high red cell count.

The testing is a complete blood count, iron studies, a reticulocyte count, hemoglobin analysis by hemoglobin electrophoresis, and gene testing.

cards.t: Treating thalassemia and the iron overload problem
q: how do you treat thalassemia
why is transfusion risky in thalassemia
why does thalassemia cause iron overload
cards.x:
Treatment is supportive: folic acid, genetic counseling, and transfusion only when absolutely necessary. Transfusion can worsen the iron overload, which is already a feature of thalassemia.

The complications to expect are iron overload (worsened by transfusion), extramedullary hematopoiesis, and hydrops fetalis. The most severe genotype is incompatible with life.

cards.t: Sickle cell anemia: hemoglobin S and why cells sickle
q: what is sickle cell anemia
why do red cells sickle
why is sickle cell trait protective against malaria
cards.x:
Sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation of a beta globin gene. Hemoglobin S is two alpha globins and two mutant beta globins. Under low oxygen tension, it polymerizes (links into chains) and the cell forms a sickle shape. Those cells block small vessels, which causes the microvascular occlusion and infarction behind the disease.

Its distribution follows the malaria belt closely. People who carry one sickle gene (sickle cell trait) are 90% less likely to have severe malaria than people with only normal hemoglobin.

cards.t: Screening for sickle cell disease in four periods
q: when is sickle cell screened for
what are the four sickle cell screening periods
what happens to affected children who miss newborn screening
cards.x:
Screening happens in four periods.

- Preconception: identify the parents whose children would be at risk.
- Prenatal: chorionic villus sampling.
- Neonatal: done now in all 50 states.
- Post-natal.

Affected children who test negative or bypass screening usually present within the first two years.

cards.t: Sickle cell in infants and its main manifestations
q: what are the symptoms of sickle cell disease
when do sickle cell symptoms start
how common is stroke in sickle cell disease
what is a pain crisis
cards.x:
Symptoms usually start around 5 months, when fetal hemoglobin gives way to hemoglobin S. Infants have failure to thrive, pain, anemia, splenomegaly, multiple chronic infections, and swelling of the hands and feet from vaso-occlusion (blockage of small blood vessels).

The main manifestations:

- Anemia: almost universal, with a hematocrit usually 15 to 30%.
- Pain crisis: from microvascular occlusions, with acute pain, tenderness, anxiety and tachycardia.
- Infarction of any tissue with vascular beds: splenic infarct, aseptic necrosis especially of the femoral or humeral heads, retinopathy and kidney disease.
- Stroke in children, 300 times higher than in unaffected children. 25% of patients have a stroke by age 45.
- Increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria.

cards.t: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease
k: leading cause of death sickle cell
q: what is acute chest syndrome
what imaging do you get first for acute chest syndrome
what causes acute chest syndrome
cards.x:
Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, often together with an acute pain event, and mortality is above 10% in adults. Its cause is multifactorial: infection, infarction, pulmonary embolism and fat embolism. Reactive lung disease increases the risk.

Consider it when there is chest pain, fever, shortness of breath, signs of a respiratory illness, hypoxemia, and pulmonary infiltrates on a chest X-ray.

A chest X-ray is the first imaging study if you suspect acute chest syndrome.

cards.t: Complications of sickle cell disease by organ
q: what are the complications of sickle cell disease
which organs are affected in sickle cell disease
what eye problems occur in sickle cell disease
cards.x:
Sickle cell complications can be acute or chronic and affect nearly every organ, head to foot:

- Brain: neurocognitive dysfunction, meningitis, stroke.
- Eye: retinopathy, post-hyphema glaucoma, retinal infarction.
- Lung: pulmonary hypertension, acute chest syndrome, acute pain event.
- Liver and gallbladder: indirect hyperbilirubinemia, sickle hepatopathy, gallstones.
- Heart: cardiomegaly, diastolic heart failure.
- Blood: anemia, leukocytosis, septicemia.
- Kidney: albuminuria, isosthenuria, kidney injury, papillary necrosis.
- Spleen: functional asplenia, splenic infarction, splenic sequestration.
- Reproductive: delayed puberty, erectile dysfunction, priapism, complications of pregnancy.
- Bone and skin: avascular necrosis, bone marrow infarction, osteomyelitis, skin ulcers, and chronic pain.

cards.t: Hemoglobin C and hemoglobin SC disease
q: what is hemoglobin C
what is hemoglobin SC disease
how severe is sickle cell SC disease
cards.x:
Hemoglobin C comes from a different mutation in the beta globin gene, and hemoglobin C does not polymerize. Inheriting one beta-C globin and one beta-S globin combines the two mutations.

That combination generally has a course between sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait, since the C hemoglobin does not polymerize the way the S one does.

cards.t: Fetal hemoglobin and its protective effect
q: what is fetal hemoglobin
why does fetal hemoglobin lessen sickle cell severity
what is hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin
cards.x:
Fetal hemoglobin is made of two alpha and two gamma globins and is normally below 1%. Some people have hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, and the amount varies.

A fetal hemoglobin level of 10 to 20% seems to be a threshold for decreased severity of sickle cell disease or beta thalassemia.

cards.t: Managing sickle cell disease
q: how do you manage sickle cell disease
what does hydroxyurea do in sickle cell disease
which symptoms need urgent assessment in sickle cell disease
cards.x:
Management has five parts.

- Disease modification: hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin and reduces vaso-occlusive events.
- Red flags: fever, chest pain or hypoxemia, or a new neurologic deficit need urgent assessment.
- Prevention: vaccinations, childhood penicillin prophylaxis when indicated, and infection education.
- Complications: transfusion or exchange for selected severe events, while monitoring for alloimmunization and iron loading.
- Long term: hematology follow-up, organ surveillance, and consideration of curative therapies.

Prevention and emergency care vary with age, genotype and clinical history.

cards.t: Hemochromatosis: primary and secondary iron overload
q: what is hemochromatosis
what is the difference between primary and secondary hemochromatosis
what organs does hemochromatosis damage
cards.x:
Hemochromatosis is iron overload: excess iron deposited throughout the body. It is asymptomatic early on. Over time the iron deposition causes oxidative stress, fibrosis and organ dysfunction, most commonly in the liver, heart, joints, endocrine organs and skin.

- Primary: an autosomal recessive disorder of the genes that control iron absorption.
- Secondary: excessive iron supplementation, chronic liver disease, or anemia, including transfusion in thalassemia.

Remember the split: primary is inherited, and secondary comes from other causes such as extra iron intake, chronic liver disease or anemia.

cards.t: Signs and symptoms of hemochromatosis
k: second and third MCP joint pain
q: what are the symptoms of hemochromatosis
why does hemochromatosis cause skin bronzing
which joints are affected in hemochromatosis
cards.x:
Symptoms depend on the organ affected.

- General: fatigue.
- Skin: bronzing of the face, neck, groin, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms and lower legs.
- Joints: pain, especially in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and the knees.
- Heart: cardiomyopathy, chest pain and dyspnea on exertion.
- Endocrine: see the pituitary effect below.

The distinctive clues are the bronzed skin and the pain in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints.

cards.t: Iron in the pituitary: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
q: why does hemochromatosis cause low libido
what endocrine problem does hemochromatosis cause
what exam findings go with pituitary iron deposition
cards.x: Iron deposited in the pituitary causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, meaning the pituitary no longer drives the sex organs properly. The symptoms are decreased libido, impotence or amenorrhea. On exam, look for small testes, gynecomastia and reduced body hair.

cards.t: Diagnosing hemochromatosis: iron panel and genetic testing
q: how do you diagnose hemochromatosis
what ferritin and transferrin saturation rule out iron overload
who should be screened for hemochromatosis
cards.x:
The diagnosis starts with the iron panel. A ferritin below 300 micrograms per liter and a transferrin saturation below 45% means no iron overload. A ferritin at or above 300 or a transferrin saturation at or above 45% means overload is possible.

Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so interpret it with the entire lab picture. Consider genetic testing (HFE gene testing) in appropriate patients with an elevated transferrin saturation or ferritin, and offer screening to first-degree relatives. HFE hemochromatosis usually presents in adults.

cards.t: Liver biopsy: primary versus secondary hemochromatosis
q: how do you tell primary from secondary hemochromatosis on biopsy
what do Kupffer cells show in hemochromatosis
what is Prussian blue stain used for
cards.x:
A liver biopsy with Prussian blue stain shows where the iron has gone.

- Primary hemochromatosis: iron accumulates in the liver cells (hepatocytes), with sparing of the Kupffer cells until later in the disease.
- Secondary hemochromatosis, from parenteral iron overload: iron accumulates predominantly in the Kupffer cells.

Quick way to tell them apart: primary spares the Kupffer cells at first, while secondary loads them.

cards.t: Treating hemochromatosis
q: how do you treat hemochromatosis
when is chelation used in hemochromatosis
what should hemochromatosis patients avoid
cards.x:
For primary disease the treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy, with ferritin-guided follow-up. For secondary overload, treat the cause and consider chelation when phlebotomy is unsuitable.

Educate the patient to avoid iron supplements and excessive alcohol, and individualize dietary advice. Offer first-degree relatives screening.

Early treatment can prevent organ damage. Assess for fibrosis and monitor cirrhosis for liver cancer, and be aware that established cirrhosis may persist.

cards.t: Therapeutic phlebotomy for hemochromatosis
q: how is primary hemochromatosis treated
what is therapeutic phlebotomy
when is chelation used instead of phlebotomy
cards.x:
The treatment to know for primary hemochromatosis is therapeutic phlebotomy, meaning blood is removed on purpose as a treatment. Follow-up is guided by the ferritin.

Secondary iron overload is handled differently. Treat the cause, and consider chelation (a drug that binds iron) when phlebotomy is unsuitable.

Alongside treatment, the patient should avoid iron supplements and excessive alcohol, dietary advice is individualized, and first-degree relatives should be offered screening. Early treatment can prevent organ damage.

cards.t: Prognosis and follow-up of each anemia at a glance
q: what is the prognosis of each type of anemia
which anemias resolve once the cause is fixed
which anemias are lifelong
cards.x:
Each anemia has its own follow-up and outlook.

- Iron deficiency: identify blood loss and reinforce iron use. It usually resolves once the cause and iron stores are corrected.
- Chronic disease: treat inflammation. It can persist while the underlying disease is active.
- Sideroblastic: remove triggers. The outlook is variable, and clonal forms may need continued follow-up.
- Megaloblastic: treat vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate deficiency. Counts improve, but delayed vitamin B12 treatment may leave deficits.
- Aplastic: urgent hematology and precautions. It depends on severity and response.
- Kidney disease: monitor hemoglobin, iron and blood pressure. It is often chronic and may improve with iron or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent.
- Sickle cell: vaccines and fever or chest pain precautions. It is a lifelong disease, and prevention reduces complications.

cards.t: Outlook of thalassemia, G6PD deficiency, autoimmune hemolysis, hemochromatosis
q: what is the outlook of thalassemia
what is the prognosis of G6PD deficiency
does autoimmune hemolytic anemia relapse
cards.x:
The other conditions in this group follow different paths.

- Thalassemia: hematology for severe forms, iron monitoring and genetic counseling. The trait is often mild, and severe forms need lifelong monitoring.
- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: avoid oxidative triggers, and seek care for jaundice or dark urine. The outlook is usually favorable with trigger avoidance.
- Autoimmune hemolysis: treat the cause, and monitor for relapse and thrombosis. Relapse may occur, and the outcome depends on cause and response.
- Hemochromatosis: iron monitoring or phlebotomy, family screening, and avoiding excess iron. Early care limits injury, though established cirrhosis may persist.

cards.t: Anemia and iron overload across the lifespan: infants to the elderly
q: what anemia problems do each age group get
how does care of anemia differ in children and the elderly
what should you check in an adolescent with heavy periods
cards.x:
Each age group has its own focus.

- Infants: use neonatal complete blood count ranges, recognize inherited anemias and abnormal newborn screens, and coordinate pediatric hematology.
- Child: assess diet and inherited anemia, consider rare genetic or transfusion-related iron overload, and use weight-based treatment.
- Adolescent: with heavy menses, check the complete blood count and ferritin, treat iron deficiency and control the bleeding, and support adherence and the transition to adult care.
- Adult: evaluate gastrointestinal and gynecologic blood loss, pregnancy and chronic kidney disease. the gene-related type of hemochromatosis usually presents in adults, so screen the family.
- Elderly: check for iron and vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, chronic kidney disease, drugs and marrow disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, and tailor treatment to function, comorbidities and goals.
